extracted.intended_audience: aspiring TV comedy writers / screenwriters preparing a comedy pilot
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for developing a full-length television comedy pilot script, covering concept/logline, characters, outlines, three-act structure, tone, comedy density, and market-readiness. Presented as a 6-week workshop with weekly assignments and instructor notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong comedic voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Am I using a strong comedic voice?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The course emphasizes developing a distinct comedic voice that carries through the pilot. Lectures and notes will help refine voice; instructors evaluate voice in critique of assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jokes per page / comedic density
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there enough jokes per page?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess density of humor across pages so the pilot reads as consistently funny. Instructor feedback across weekly assignments will flag under- or over-burdened pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters are funny and relatable
rubrics_metrics.description: Are my characters funny and relatable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor will explain how to build characters, what each character needs, and assigning them roles within the narrative. Character bios and their roles are critiqued to ensure humor and relatability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelling central theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a compelling central theme?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pilot should have an identifiable thematic core that shapes story and character choices; lectures cover how theme supports both comedy and series potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engaging, well-structured story
rubrics_metrics.description: Am I telling an engaging, well-structured story?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course teaches outlines, common formats, and the 3-act comedy structure. Weekly breakdowns move from concept to outline to full acts, with instructor notes to improve story engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall hilarity / tonal success
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it hilarious? (or if it's a dark comedy) Is it insanely sad... and also hilarious?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates whether the pilot achieves its intended comedic effect or, for dark comedy, balances sadness and humor. Tone and emotional mixture will be examined in lectures and critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear concept and logline
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor will explain loglines and how to structure them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concise, marketable logline that communicates concept and stakes is required; logline and concept are early assignments and receive instructor notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline quality and use of formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor will introduce outlines and discuss structure and common formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlines should clearly lay out beats, acts, and story flow using industry-appropriate formats; students receive feedback on outline assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of Cold Open / Teaser / Tag
rubrics_metrics.description: Break down the 3-act comedy structure including the roles of Cold Open/Teasers and tags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective placement and function of teasers and tags to hook viewers and close scenes are reviewed with examples and notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone consistency based on genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor will discuss the importance of tone based on the genres of the comedy pilots being written in class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone must suit the sub-genre (e.g., single-camera vs. multicam, dark comedy vs. broad comedy). Lectures address tone choices and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and market awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Importance of researching similar genre shows and give examples to class participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should research comparable shows to understand market positioning, tone, and structure; instructor provides examples and discusses buyers/sub-genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict and set-up in Act One
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss the importance of conflict, set-up, and how to not be too exposition-heavy in the first act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act One should establish conflict and character quickly without excessive exposition; instructor critiques first-act drafts for balance and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rising action and Act Two climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor will discuss the importance of rising action, the act two climax (reversals, complications, reveals, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act Two must escalate stakes and include a satisfying midpoint/act-two climax using reversals and complications; examples and notes guide execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act Three conclusion and series setup
rubrics_metrics.description: Importance of the conclusion of the pilot while also setting up the conflict for the entire series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pilot's ending should resolve the episode's story while opening an overarching plot for future seasons; lectures and critiques focus on balancing closure with series potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding exposition-heavy writing
rubrics_metrics.description: How to not be too exposition-heavy in the first act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques for showing vs telling, integrating character information organically, and pacing exposition are covered and applied to Act One assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receptiveness to notes / revision capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Each week, Michael will critique the writers' assignments personally, and give notes on how best to move forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability to absorb and implement instructor feedback across successive assignments is an implicit criterion; students get individual notes and a final one-on-one consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliverable: complete, market-ready pilot draft
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave this 6-week course with a first draft of your TV Comedy Pilot ready to market!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By course end students should have a full pilot script and a final 20-minute consultation discussing final notes and how to get it out to the marketplace; readiness for submission/marketing is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and assignment completion
rubrics_metrics.description: Weekly assignments (logline, character bios, outline, acts) and participation in Q&A sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students must complete prep assignments and weekly deliverables to receive personalized notes; instructor reviews submitted materials and provides guidance during class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry context and buyer awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor will talk about the current state of TV Comedy in the industry: types, sub-genres, buyers, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the marketplace, different buyer expectations, and where a pilot fits helps shape creative and marketing decisions; lectures address these industry realities.
